analogy.p: Imagine metals as people in a queue to hold a hand of electrons (a 'seat') in a compound, ranked by how strongly they want to give up electrons and join the crowd of positive ions. A more reactive metal is like a stronger person who barges in and pushes a weaker person out of the seat: the weaker one is left standing alone as a solid metal. This maps correctly because a more reactive metal forms ions more easily and displaces the less reactive metal from solution. It breaks down because real displacement involves electron transfer and not just pushing: the electrons move from one atom to another ion, and the energy released is a real chemical energy change.
analogy.t: A queue for the last seat

bullets: **Most reactive at the top:** potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium react with cold water; gold, at the bottom, is so unreactive it is found as the metal itself ('native') in the ground.
A common memory sentence: **P**lease **S**top **L**ending **C**alcium **M**y **A**unt **C**arbon **Z**ebras **I**n **H**er **C**oat **S**ilver **G**old.

**Carbon and hydrogen** are not metals in this context but are placed in the series because they are used as comparisons: carbon decides whether a metal can be extracted by heating with carbon, and hydrogen decides whether a metal reacts with dilute acid to release hydrogen.
The series was worked out from **experimental evidence**: how vigorously metals react with oxygen, water and acids, and which metals displace which from solutions of their salts.
Position in the series is closely linked to how easily a metal **loses electrons to form positive ions** (cations): the higher the metal, the more easily it does this.
Used to: predict reactions, explain observations, choose extraction methods (see the extraction of metals note), and choose metals for jobs such as sacrificial protection of iron.
Exam use: you are often given experimental results and asked to **deduce the order of reactivity**, so the series is a tool for reasoning, not only recall.
core.h: What the reactivity series is and why it matters
core.p: The **reactivity series** is a league table that lists metals (plus carbon and hydrogen for comparison) in order of how readily they react. A metal high in the series reacts more vigorously with oxygen, water and acids than a metal low in the series. The series is not just a list to memorise: it lets you predict whether a reaction will happen, which metal will be displaced, and later in the course how a metal can be extracted from its ore. The order you must recall is potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold.

bullets: General word equation: **metal + oxygen → metal oxide**.
Magnesium: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (bright white flame, white solid ash). Very exothermic.
Aluminium: 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3. Copper: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO (black solid on heated copper).
Zinc and iron also form oxides when heated (iron wool glows and forms iron oxide).

**Aluminium looks unreactive in everyday life** although it is high in the series. This is because a thin, tough, **protective layer of aluminium oxide** forms instantly on the surface and stops oxygen, water and many acids reaching the metal underneath. It reacts more as expected once this layer is removed.
The reaction with oxygen is oxidation: the metal atoms **lose electrons** to oxygen, forming metal ions (for example Mg2+) and oxide ions (O2-).
Gold does not react with oxygen, which is why it stays shiny and is used in jewellery and electronic contacts.
core.p: Metals react with oxygen to form **metal oxides**. This is an **oxidation** reaction because the metal gains oxygen. The more reactive the metal, the more vigorously it reacts: magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame to leave white magnesium oxide, while copper only turns black on its surface when heated strongly, and gold does not react at all. Many metals are covered with a thin layer of oxide at all times, which is why metals such as aluminium look dull until polished.

bullets: General equation: **metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**, for example 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2 and 2K + 2H2O → 2KOH + H2.
Lithium: 2Li + 2H2O → 2LiOH + H2. Calcium: Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2.
**Potassium:** reacts violently, moves quickly over the surface, melts, and the hydrogen burns with a **lilac flame**.

**Sodium:** fizzes rapidly, melts into a ball because the reaction is exothermic and sodium has a low melting point, moves around on the surface and gets smaller. **Lithium:** fizzes steadily, floats, moves around but does not melt.
**Calcium:** sinks, fizzes steadily, the water becomes cloudy and warm as calcium hydroxide is not very soluble.

**Magnesium:** reacts only very slowly with cold water (a few bubbles over a long time) but reacts quickly with **steam**: Mg + H2O → MgO + H2, burning with a bright white flame to give white magnesium oxide.
**Zinc** and **iron** react with steam only (slowly, and iron reversibly), forming the metal oxide and hydrogen. **Copper** does not react with water or steam.
core.p: The metals at the top of the series react with **cold water** to produce a **metal hydroxide** and **hydrogen gas**. The hydroxides of potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium dissolve to give an **alkaline solution** (pH above 7; universal indicator turns purple or blue). Less reactive metals react with water only when it is steam, and then they form the metal oxide instead of the hydroxide. Metals low in the series do not react with water at all. The speed of the reaction is how we rank the metals.

bullets: General word equation: **metal + acid → salt + hydrogen**.
Magnesium: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2 (very rapid fizzing, test tube gets warm, metal disappears quickly).
Zinc: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2 (steady fizzing, noticeably slower than magnesium).
Iron: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2 (slow bubbling; a pale green iron(II) salt forms). Note iron forms iron(II), not iron(III), here.
Copper: **no reaction** with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, because copper is less reactive than hydrogen.
Test for the gas: hold a **lit splint** at the mouth of the test tube. Hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop**.
Ionic equation for a metal such as magnesium: **Mg + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2**. Chloride ions are spectators.
Very reactive metals (potassium, sodium) are never added to acid in school labs because the reaction is dangerously violent.
core.h: Reactions of metals with dilute acids
core.p: Metals that are above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids (such as dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid) to give a **salt** and **hydrogen gas**. The metal atoms displace the hydrogen from the acid: each metal atom loses electrons to hydrogen ions. The more reactive the metal, the faster the bubbles appear and the more heat is released. Metals below hydrogen, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids.

bullets: Quantitative approaches: measure **temperature rise** (thermometer) or **volume of hydrogen** collected in a gas syringe against time, or time taken for the metal to disappear.
Control variables: same **mass or surface area** of metal (ribbon of equal length, or powder of equal mass), same **volume and concentration of acid**, same starting **temperature**.
Why surface area matters: a powder has more surface exposed so reacts faster than a lump of the same metal, which could wrongly make an unreactive powder look more reactive than a reactive strip.
Safety: wear **eye protection**; use small pieces of reactive metals; keep flames away from hydrogen; use dilute acid.
Sensible ranking from experiments: magnesium (very fast) > zinc (moderate) > iron (slow) > copper (none).
Among Group 1 metals: **Li < Na < K** in reactivity because going down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
Always link back: faster reaction = **more reactive** = loses electrons more easily.
core.p: Reactivity is ranked using observations: how fast bubbles are produced, how quickly the metal disappears, whether it melts, whether a flame is seen, and how much the temperature rises. In a fair test you compare metals under identical conditions and the metal giving the fastest, most vigorous change is placed highest. Observations should always be **specific**: 'rapid fizzing and the test tube becomes hot' earns credit while 'it reacted quickly' usually does not.

bullets: Metal atoms form ions such as Na+, Mg2+, Al3+, Zn2+, Fe2+, Cu2+ by losing electrons.
Examples of half equations: Na → Na+ + e-, Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-, Al → Al3+ + 3e-.

The number of electrons lost does **not** decide reactivity: sodium loses only one electron but is far more reactive than aluminium, which loses three. What matters is **how easily** electrons are lost.
Reactive metals form ions easily so their compounds are very **stable**: they are hard to break down, which is why extraction of reactive metals needs electrolysis.
Unreactive metals (such as gold) rarely form ions, so they are found uncombined in nature.
The ease of forming ions is what makes a more reactive metal push a less reactive one out of its compound in displacement.
Link to other topics: Group 1 trends (reactivity increases down the group), electrolysis, and the extraction of metals.
core.h: Why reactivity is about losing electrons
core.p: When a metal reacts, its atoms lose electrons from their outer shell and become positively charged **ions (cations)**. The **reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form positive ions**. A metal high in the series loses electrons very readily, so it reacts quickly and vigorously, while a metal low in the series holds on to its electrons and forms ions reluctantly. This idea turns the series from a list into an explanation, and it is the key to understanding displacement, oxidation and reduction and electrolysis.

bullets: General word equation: **more reactive metal + salt of less reactive metal → salt of more reactive metal + less reactive metal**.
Displacement is possible only if the added metal is **higher in the reactivity series** than the metal in the compound.

Displacement can also happen with metal **oxides**: a more reactive metal can take oxygen from a less reactive metal oxide (for example the thermite reaction 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe, very exothermic, used to weld railway lines).
Carbon can displace metals below it from their oxides, which is the basis of extraction of iron (see the extraction of metals note).
Observations signalling displacement: a **colour change** in the solution, a **solid deposit** on the metal, and often a **temperature rise** because displacement reactions are exothermic.
If nothing happens (no colour change, no deposit, no temperature change), the added metal is **less reactive**.
Metals in solution should be as salts that dissolve: nitrates, sulfates and chlorides are used.
core.p: A **displacement reaction** happens when a **more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound**. The more reactive metal is better at forming positive ions, so it pushes the less reactive metal out of solution and the less reactive metal is left as the solid element. If the metal added is less reactive than the metal already in the compound, **no reaction** happens. By testing several metals against several metal salt solutions you can build up the order of reactivity.

bullets: **Magnesium + copper sulfate:** Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu. The blue solution fades to colourless, a **brown/pink solid (copper)** forms, and the mixture warms.
**Zinc + copper sulfate:** Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu. Same observations but slower than magnesium.
**Iron + copper sulfate:** Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu. The blue solution turns pale green and brown copper coats the iron nail.
**Copper + silver nitrate:** Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag. Silver crystals form (often grey, feathery) and the solution turns blue as copper(II) ions form.
**Zinc + iron sulfate:** Zn + FeSO4 → ZnSO4 + Fe (pale green solution fades, grey solid iron forms).
**No reaction:** copper + zinc sulfate, iron + magnesium sulfate, silver + copper sulfate. Write 'no reaction' because the added metal is less reactive.
State symbols: (s) for the solid metal, (aq) for solutions, so for example Mg(s) + CuSO4(aq) → MgSO4(aq) + Cu(s).
core.p: You need to be able to give word equations, balanced symbol equations and observations for common displacement reactions. Three standard examples are magnesium or zinc or iron with copper(II) sulfate solution, and copper with silver nitrate solution. In each case a coloured solution fades and a coloured solid appears. Practise writing each one in words, then symbols with state symbols, then as an ionic equation.

bullets: From Mg(s) + CuSO4(aq) → MgSO4(aq) + Cu(s), write the soluble compounds as ions: Mg + Cu2+ + SO4 2- → Mg2+ + SO4 2- + Cu.
Cancel the spectator ion (SO4 2-) from both sides: **Mg(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + Cu(s)**.
Check balance: total charge on the left is 2+ and on the right is 2+; there is one Mg and one Cu atom on each side.
Zinc and iron nails: Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu and Fe + Cu2+ → Fe2+ + Cu.
Copper and silver nitrate: **Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag** (two silver ions are needed to take the two electrons from one copper atom).
With acid: Mg + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2, the metal displaces hydrogen from the acid.
Common mistake: leaving the spectator ions in, or forgetting that charge must balance.
core.p: An **ionic equation** shows only the particles that actually change in a reaction. In a displacement reaction in solution the metal atoms of the solid and the metal ions in the solution are the only things that change. The negative ions (such as sulfate or nitrate) stay dissolved and unchanged throughout; they are called **spectator ions** and are left out. Writing ionic equations shows clearly what is oxidised and what is reduced, and the charges must balance as well as the atoms.

bullets: Oxidation half-equation: **Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-** (magnesium loses electrons, it is oxidised).
Reduction half-equation: **Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu** (copper ions gain electrons, they are reduced).
Add the half-equations and cancel the electrons to get the ionic equation: Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu.
In terms of oxygen only: oxidation is gain of oxygen and reduction is loss of oxygen, but for reactions of ions in solution you must use the **electron definition**.
The reactant that loses electrons is the **reducing agent**; the one that gains electrons is the **oxidising agent** (not required by name but useful for reasoning).
With acids, the metal is oxidised and the hydrogen ions are reduced: 2H+ + 2e- → H2.
Link: the same electron idea explains why reactive metals must be extracted by electrolysis (adding electrons to the metal ions).
core.h: Oxidation and reduction in displacement (electron transfer)
core.p: Displacement reactions are examples of **redox reactions**, in which both **oxidation** and **reduction** happen at the same time. In terms of electrons, **oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons** (remember **OIL RIG**: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). In Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu the magnesium atom loses two electrons, so it is oxidised, and the copper ion gains those two electrons, so it is reduced. The more reactive metal is always oxidised, and the ion of the less reactive metal is reduced.

bullets: Step 1: list each piece of evidence as 'X is more reactive than Y'.
Step 2: link them: if A > B and B > C then A > B > C.
Step 3: use acid results to place metals relative to hydrogen: reacts with dilute acid = above H; no reaction = below H.
Step 4: use displacement results for fine detail between two metals.
A **vigorous** observation (rapid fizzing, large temperature rise, flame) means higher reactivity than a slow observation (few bubbles).
If a metal appears in the 'displaces' column but not the 'displaced' column, it is at the top of the group tested; the reverse puts it at the bottom.
The diagonal of a results grid (a metal with its own salt) is always blank, because a metal cannot displace itself.
core.h: Deducing an order of reactivity from experimental results
core.p: Exam questions often give a table of observations from several metals reacting with water, acid or each other's salt solutions and ask you to rank them. The method is to look for the metal that reacts the most vigorously, or the metal that displaces others, and work down from there. If metal A displaces metal B from its salt solution, then A is more reactive than B. If a metal reacts with dilute acid but another does not, the one that reacts is above hydrogen and the other below. Combine every piece of information to produce a complete order, and explain it in a sentence.

bullets: Reactions with carbon: iron(III) oxide + carbon → iron + carbon dioxide (2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2); zinc oxide and copper oxide can be reduced by carbon too.
Metals above carbon (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al) form very stable compounds, so they are extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound.
Reduction here means **loss of oxygen**: the metal oxide is reduced, and carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide or carbon dioxide.
Hydrogen divides metals into those that react with dilute acids (above) and those that do not (below).
Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen, so they do not release hydrogen from dilute acids; gold and sometimes silver and copper occur uncombined in the Earth.

Link to **Earth's resources**: unreactive metals are mined as the element or easy to extract; reactive metals needed more energy-hungry methods, which explains why aluminium was expensive until electrolysis was developed.
Link to **corrosion prevention**: zinc, being more reactive than iron, is used in galvanising and as a sacrificial metal because it corrodes in preference to iron.
core.h: Carbon, hydrogen and the link to extraction
core.p: Carbon and hydrogen are included in the reactivity series even though they are non-metals because they behave as if they were metals in reactions where they compete for oxygen or for combining with other elements. Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc. A metal below carbon in the series can be extracted from its oxide by **heating with carbon**, because carbon is more reactive and displaces the metal by taking away the oxygen. Metals above carbon cannot be extracted that way because carbon is less reactive than them, and need **electrolysis**. Hydrogen sits between iron and copper and marks the boundary of metals that react with dilute acids.

bullets: **Method (acid):** add the same volume of the same dilute acid to a test tube or beaker for each metal; measure the starting temperature; add equal-sized pieces of metal; record the highest temperature or time for fizzing to stop.

**Method (displacement):** add a few cm3 of each salt solution to separate test tubes or the wells of a spotting tile; add a small piece of each metal; leave for a few minutes and record any colour change or solid forming; draw a results table.

**Independent variable:** the metal. **Dependent variable:** temperature change, volume or rate of gas, or observed change. **Controls:** acid or solution concentration and volume, metal size and surface area, starting temperature.
Make it more precise: use a **gas syringe** to measure hydrogen volume at set times, or a thermometer in an insulated polystyrene cup.
**Safety:** eye protection; handle metals with tweezers; keep reactive metals (Na, K, Li, Ca) for teacher demonstration; take care with hot test tubes; avoid naked flames near hydrogen.
**Reliability:** repeat and calculate a mean; do not take anomalies into account unless the cause is identified.
Table headings should include units, for example 'Temperature rise (°C)'.
core.p: You may be asked to describe, evaluate or improve an experiment to compare the reactivity of metals. A typical investigation places equal-sized pieces of different metals into the same volume of dilute acid and observes or measures what happens, or places the metals in test tubes of metal salt solutions and records observations. A good answer names the independent variable (the metal), the dependent variable (a measured change such as temperature rise or volume of gas) and the control variables, and mentions risks and how to reduce them.

bullets: Prediction pattern: 'X is more reactive than Y, so X displaces Y from its compound'.
Typical 3-mark answer: states that magnesium is more reactive than copper (1), magnesium displaces copper from solution (1), brown solid forms and blue colour fades (1).
Typical 4-mark answer adds the ionic equation or the electron transfer: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e- and Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.
If asked 'why does aluminium appear unreactive?' answer in terms of the **protective oxide layer**.
If asked 'why is sodium kept under oil?' answer: it is very reactive with air and water, and oil prevents contact.
Use the series to predict gas production: metals above hydrogen produce hydrogen with acids; those below do not.
Be ready to apply the same reasoning to unfamiliar metals (e.g. 'metal X displaces iron but not magnesium, so X is between Mg and Fe').
core.h: Putting it together: predicting and explaining
core.p: To score full marks you need to move smoothly between observation, equation and explanation. Start from the reactivity series, decide which species is higher, predict whether anything happens, then describe what is seen and write the equation. Finally give the reason, always in terms of reactivity or the tendency to lose electrons. This final step is what separates a grade 5 answer from a grade 8 or 9 answer.

exam: **Describe/State (1-2 marks):** short factual statements: 'bubbles', 'metal gets smaller', 'solution turns pale green'. Use the exact observation, never 'it reacts'.
**Name the gas / test (2 marks):** hydrogen, lit splint, squeaky pop. The test AND the result are both needed.
**Word equations (1-2 marks):** metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Get the correct salt: hydrochloric gives chloride, sulfuric gives sulfate, nitric gives nitrate.
**Balanced symbol equations (2-3 marks):** correct formulae first, then balance; state symbols are often optional but add them if asked.
**Order of reactivity from data (2-3 marks):** give the full order, with the most reactive first, and justify with 'most vigorous reaction' or 'displaces X from solution'.
**Explain displacement (2-4 marks):** 'X is more reactive than Y' (1), 'so X displaces Y from its compound/solution' (1), observation (1), electron transfer (1).
**Oxidised/reduced (2 marks):** use electrons: 'Mg loses electrons so it is oxidised; Cu2+ gains electrons so it is reduced'.
**Ionic equation (2 marks):** spectator ions removed, charges and atoms balance.
**Method/evaluate (up to 6 marks):** state the independent, dependent and control variables, give equipment, hazards and how to improve reliability. Use linked sentences with the word 'because'.
**Why questions:** always finish with tendency to lose electrons or protective oxide layer. 'Because it is more reactive' alone earns only 1 mark.
**Graph/data tips:** read the question carefully for units; for temperature rise subtract start temperature from highest temperature.

mistakes.r: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but reacts quickly with steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen.
mistakes.w: Magnesium does not react with water.

mistakes.r: Metal atoms **lose** electrons to form positive ions; this is oxidation.
mistakes.w: Metals gain electrons when they react.

mistakes.r: Copper is below hydrogen in the series, so there is **no reaction** with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
mistakes.w: Copper reacts with dilute acid to give hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Aluminium is above carbon but is protected by a thin layer of aluminium oxide on its surface.
mistakes.w: Aluminium is unreactive because it is low in the series.

mistakes.r: Iron forms iron(II) chloride, FeCl2: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2.
mistakes.w: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid to give iron(III) chloride (FeCl3).

mistakes.r: Sulfate ions are spectator ions; only the metal atoms and metal ions change.
mistakes.w: In a displacement reaction the sulfate ions react.

mistakes.r: Reactivity depends on how easily electrons are lost, not how many; sodium loses one electron more easily than aluminium loses three.
mistakes.w: The metal with more electrons lost is more reactive (aluminium loses 3 so it beats sodium).

mistakes.r: The metal is displaced as a solid; for copper, a brown/pink solid forms and the blue colour of the solution fades.
mistakes.w: The metal 'dissolves and the solution turns brown'.

mistakes.r: Magnesium is more reactive than copper so it displaces copper: Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu.
mistakes.w: Magnesium + copper sulfate → magnesium + copper sulfate (no change).

summary: You must recall the reactivity series (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au) and describe how the metals react with oxygen, water and dilute acids. You must predict and explain displacement reactions, write ionic equations and say which species is oxidised and reduced. It matters because the series predicts reactions and underpins metal extraction.

terms.d: A list of metals (with carbon and hydrogen for comparison) in order of their reactivity, from most reactive to least reactive.
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen).
Gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen).
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction both happen.
A compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen.
A compound containing a metal ion and hydroxide ions, formed when reactive metals react with water.
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal (or ammonium) ion.
A positively charged ion, formed when a metal atom loses electrons.
An equation showing only the ions or particles that change in a reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An ion that is present but does not take part in a reaction and is unchanged.
An equation showing the loss or gain of electrons by one species, for example Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-.
Water in its gaseous state, used to react with less reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc and iron.
A solution containing excess OH- ions with pH greater than 7.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
A thin, unreactive layer of metal oxide that covers a metal and stops further reaction, as on aluminium.
A substance that reduces another by giving electrons to it, being oxidised itself.
A more reactive metal attached to iron so that it corrodes instead of the iron.

worked.ans: (a) W > Z > Y > X. (b) No reaction, because Y is less reactive than Z, so it cannot displace Z from its sulfate solution.
worked.q: Four metals W, X, Y and Z were added to dilute hydrochloric acid. W: vigorous fizzing, test tube hot. X: no bubbles. Y: a few slow bubbles. Z: steady bubbles, faster than Y. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (2 marks) (b) Metal Y is added to a solution of the sulfate of metal Z. Predict what happens and explain. (2 marks)
steps: Rank by rate of bubbles: W (most vigorous), then Z (steady), then Y (slow), then X (no reaction).
A metal that does not react with dilute acid is below hydrogen in the series, so X is least reactive.
Y is less reactive than Z because it produced bubbles more slowly.
A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its compound.

worked.ans: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s); ionic: Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu. Zinc atoms lose electrons (oxidised); copper ions gain electrons (reduced).
worked.q: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. (a) Write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols. (b) Write the ionic equation. (c) Explain, in terms of electrons, which species is oxidised and which is reduced. (4 marks)
steps: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it.
(b) Spectator ion is SO4 2-: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s).
(c) Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- : zinc loses electrons, so zinc is oxidised. Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu : copper ions gain electrons, so copper ions are reduced.

worked.q: 0.24 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure. (Ar of Mg = 24; 1 mole of gas occupies 24 dm3.) (3 marks)
steps: Moles of Mg = mass ÷ Ar = 0.24 ÷ 24 = 0.010 mol.
From the equation, 1 mol Mg gives 1 mol H2, so moles of H2 = 0.010 mol.
